results.title: INS Seed / Fast INS initialization
results.content: + System start-up and alignment techniques + INS Seed / Fast INS initialization + Recommended messages to be logged for SPAN data collection + Body to vehicle frame rotation calibration routine + Multi-line body to vehicle frame rotation calibration routine Operation / SPAN GNSS+INS / Real-time operation / INS Seed / Fast INS initialization # INS Seed / Fast INS initialization The INS Seed functionality is an alignment method whereby INS alignment information from a previous powerup can be injected into the system at startup to achieve an INS alignment more quickly. When INS Seed is enabled, alignment data is automatically saved when appropriate, with no specific action required from the user. ### Saving The following criteria must be met for valid alignment data to be saved into receiver NVM. The following criteria must be met in order to use a seed: * Seed data from NVM must be valid * The system must be stationary * The system must not have moved significantly from the seed position: less than 10 metres in position and 10 degrees in heading If a valid error model is present in the seed data from NVM, this will always be used, even if the system is not stationary or exceeded the movement thresholds. Forcing an injection of an NVM seed without the validation checks can cause an unstable INS solution if the vehicle has moved. Apart from injecting the seed at start-up without validation, this will also remove some requirements typically asserted to allow the filter to converge. 3. If valid, alignment data will be injected. ## System indicators The **INSSEEDSTATUS** log reports the seed injection status for the current power up and information on current seed validity. The Extended Solution Status field in the **INSPVAX** log has bits that indicate if the alignment direction is verified, the Alignment type that occurred and NVM seed injection status. When the seed is injected and kinematic validation is finished, bit 25 is set to 1. results.title: Dropping and Lifting Anchor Procedures on Ships – Maritime Education
results.content: # Dropping and Lifting Anchor Procedures on Ships Anchoring is a critical operation in ship navigation, essential for ensuring vessel stability, safety, and operational efficiency. A well-executed anchoring procedure safeguards the ship, crew, cargo, and marine environment. This article explores the procedures involved in dropping and lifting anchors on ships, emphasizing best practices, operational guidelines, and real-world case studies to highlight the importance of this essential maritime operation. Anchoring secures a ship in place when docking at a port, awaiting berth clearance, or holding position in designated anchorages. Ships also anchor in emergencies, such as engine failures or rough weather, to avoid drifting into hazardous areas. Before initiating the anchoring process, the ship’s crew must prepare thoroughly by: * Checking the Anchor and Windlass: Inspect the windlass, chains, and brakes to ensure they are in working condition. Example: In the English Channel, ships choose sandy seabed areas to anchor securely and avoid strong tidal currents. The scope of the anchor chain is critical for ensuring the ship remains stationary. Anchor Chain Length=Water Depth+Height of Ship’s Hawsepipe Above Water×Scope Ratio (5 to 7)\text{Anchor Chain Length} = \text{Water Depth} + \text{Height of Ship’s Hawsepipe Above Water} \times \text{Scope Ratio (5 to 7)}Anchor Chain Length=Water Depth+Height of Ship’s Hawsepipe Above Water×Scope Ratio (5 to 7) Case Study: During a cargo operation delay in Singapore Anchorage, a bulk carrier used a 7:1 scope ratio to remain securely anchored amid strong tidal currents. ## — ## **Safety Considerations During Anchoring Operations** Safety is paramount during anchoring operations due to the potential for heavy equipment failures, crew injuries, or ship collisions. Case Study: Anchor Failure Incident In 2017, a container ship experienced an anchor chain failure while anchoring off the **Port of Long Beach**. ## — ## **Challenges and Mitigation in Anchoring Operations** Despite well-defined procedures, anchoring operations face challenges such as: * Strong Winds and Currents: Use extra chain length and bow thrusters to counteract strong winds. * Equipment Failure: Conduct regular maintenance of the windlass, brakes, and anchor chains. By following best practices, using proper communication, and conducting equipment maintenance, ships can anchor safely and efficiently, ensuring smooth maritime operations and environmental safety.

results.title: Anchor Windlass - Understanding Design And Operation
results.content: # Anchor Windlass – Understanding Design And Operation. A mechanical device known as the anchor windlass is used for this very purpose. Owing to this, advanced anchor windlass systems have also been used to effectively operate the anchor and associated machinery. In this article, we will examine what an anchor windlass is, and how it operates. Thus, for an anchor windlass that has to lift a weight of nearly a ton, specialized mechanisms have to be used to ensure that the weight of the anchor head is taken off the anchor rode while the operation is stalled. For medium-sized vessels, a single windlass is often used to control the anchors on the port and starboard side. This is a simple mechanism, that uses a single windlass drum to control the anchor rode for both sides. However, for larger ships that require a higher degree of precision, the anchors on both sides are given separate windlass systems. ### **How an Anchor Windlass Works**. The powered option uses the windlass to slowly revolve in a direction that pays out the anchor chain. Once the markers on the anchor chain indicate that the required length has been paid out, the crank operator can then apply a braking action to the windlass barrel. In addition, it is also possible to position the anchor head to the required location by manipulating the windlass controls. The various components that make up the anchor windlass broadly include- the winch, dog clutch, chain wheel drum, pawl bar, and hawsepipe. As discussed earlier, for reeling out the anchor rode, a crankshaft rotates the windlass drum. As the winch rotates the chain wheel, the rode is slowly paid out through the hawsepipe, which is an opening located on the side of the hull on which the anchor head sits. The manner in which the anchor windlass operates is through the following steps given below:. To obtain a factor of safety in the operation of the anchor windlass, the windlass must be able to completely raise or lower the anchor head at any speed within its given operating rpm range. By following these strict safety protocols, it is possible to safely use the windlass anchor without causing any accidents.
